title: Global Event Ordering in Distributed Inventory Systems
business: A global retail chain managing distributed inventory across multiple regional data centers.
problem: Without a shared physical clock, concurrent updates to stock levels across different regions lead to race conditions where the system cannot determine which transaction occurred first, resulting in inconsistent inventory counts.
solution: Lamport Timestamps provide a logical clock mechanism that assigns a monotonically increasing counter to every event. By attaching this counter to messages between nodes, the system establishes a partial ordering of events that respects causality, ensuring that if event A causes event B, A is guaranteed to have a lower timestamp than B.
steps: Initialize a local counter to zero on every inventory node.
Increment the local counter before executing any local inventory update.
Attach the current counter value to any inter-node synchronization message.
Upon receiving a message, update the local counter to be the maximum of the current local value and the received timestamp plus one.
Use the combined (timestamp, node_id) tuple to break ties and establish a total ordering for all inventory operations.
outcome: The system achieves a consistent causal history of inventory changes, allowing the application to resolve conflicts by identifying the true sequence of operations regardless of physical clock drift.
limitation: Lamport Timestamps establish causality but do not provide information about real-time duration or absolute time. A limitation is that they cannot determine if two events are concurrent or simply unrelated in time; this can be checked by verifying if the timestamps of two events are incomparable in the partial order.

questions.question: In Global Event Ordering in Distributed Inventory Systems, how do Lamport Timestamps resolve the problem of inconsistent inventory counts?
options: By synchronizing all server clocks to a single atomic time source.
By assigning a logical counter that respects the happened-before relationship.
By using physical hardware sensors to measure exact latency.
By rejecting all concurrent updates that arrive at the same time.
questions.explanation: Lamport Timestamps use logical counters to order events based on causality rather than physical time.
questions.evidence: Lamport Timestamps provide a logical clock mechanism that assigns a monotonically increasing counter to every event.

questions.question: What is a primary limitation of the implementation described in Global Event Ordering in Distributed Inventory Systems?
options: The counters grow too large to be stored in memory.
They require a centralized server to issue timestamps.
They cannot provide information about real-time duration or absolute time.
They fail to establish any ordering between nodes.
questions.explanation: Logical clocks track causality but lack the ability to map events to real-world wall-clock time.
questions.evidence: A limitation is that they cannot determine if two events are concurrent or simply unrelated in time; this can be checked by verifying if the timestamps of two events are incomparable in the partial order.
